claim: 63% live pay cheque to pay cheque, lack emergency savings, or have less than $500.
assessment: These are different measures. SHED reports 63% could meet a $400 expense with cash or equivalent in 2025. The transcript’s original survey is unidentified.

claim: Prices are rising faster than wages.
assessment: Use matched WPI and CPI indexes and calculate their ratio; include household living-cost indexes.

claim: Government involvement causes higher education, health and housing costs.
assessment: Compare demand subsidies with supply policy, staffing intensity, quality and demographics; co-movement alone cannot isolate causation.

claim: University administrative staff rose from 10% to 60% over 30 years.
assessment: Need original classification, institution coverage and denominator. US NCES/IPEDS and Australian Department of Education higher-education staff collections are candidate sources.

claim: Success should mean 2% a year moving from labour dependence to capital independence.
assessment: Define accessible assets, sustainable after-tax income and household essential spending. Superannuation access limits matter. No standard OECD transition series identified.

claim: 10% annual returns illustrate financial freedom and rapid compounding.
assessment: A tenfold increase at 10% takes about 24.2 years before taxes, fees and withdrawals. Average market returns are not guaranteed retirement income.

claim: Debt is paid through money creation, explaining inflation.
assessment: Separate bond issuance, central-bank purchases, private credit, demand, supply shocks and monetary-policy response.

claim: Close to half of Americans are government employees, contractors or pension recipients.
verdict: Mixed populations; not an employment rate
assessment: Employees, beneficiaries and contractors overlap. Count unique people for income exposure; use employed people as denominator for employment shares.

claim: Labour is taxed more heavily than capital, and asset-backed borrowing avoids realisation.
assessment: Compare effective lifetime tax wedges; account for company tax, imputation, inflation, realisation timing and superannuation. Borrowing creates a liability, not net wealth.

claim: California’s top 1% pays 40–50% of personal income tax.
assessment: Use California Franchise Tax Board tables for the same year; do not substitute all government revenue for personal income tax.

claim: France lost more revenue from wealth-tax migration than the tax raised.
assessment: Require French official reform evaluations, defined time period and counterfactual; distinguish migration from asset repricing.

claim: Housing wealth growth reduces access for subsequent buyers.
assessment: Use housing prices, rent, income, mortgage rates and tenure by age; total owner returns must include costs and imputed rent.

claim: 40–45 million Americans graduated over ten years and face debt and difficult jobs.
assessment: Count people rather than qualifications; US Education/NCES and Australian Education/ATO collections need consistent cohorts.

claim: China’s GDP per person grew from roughly 3,000 to 30,000 due to market freedom.
assessment: Establish currency and PPP/price basis before checking growth; China is outside the OECD membership cohort.

claim: Inequality is necessary for progress.
assessment: Compare productivity and median income with wealth shares, business formation and R&D. Test competing explanations.

claim: Career politicians and election cycles encourage excess spending.
verdict: Hypothesis; descriptive data cannot prove it
assessment: Code employment spells and tenure; test policy outcomes separately. Career background is not a competence score.

claim: Denmark offers security but little entrepreneurship or opportunity to progress.
assessment: Statistics Denmark publishes business births and high-growth enterprise statistics. Compare innovation and distribution separately; avoid equating social insurance with central planning.

claim: High spending and taxes reduce UK productivity.
assessment: Control for investment, industry mix, skills, trade and demographics; allow public infrastructure and health to improve capacity.

claim: AI improves output per hour; early-career employment may fall despite low aggregate unemployment.
assessment: Track hours, real pay, vacancies and age/occupation employment. The cited 13% estimate requires its underlying Stanford study and data; it is not a national unemployment rate.

claim: Public jobs may create less value than their wages.
assessment: Measured output and social benefit differ. Do not infer unproductive work from public funding.

claim: US wealth totals $183tn; billionaires $8tn; $50m+ households $23tn; bottom half $6tn.
assessment: Check dates, households versus people, market valuation and overlapping groups. A wealth stock is not annual revenue.

claim: Public retirement arrangements are unreliable; asset ownership offers a better route.
assessment: US Social Security, defined-benefit schemes and Australian superannuation are different. Compare replacement rates, funded assets, risk and access.

claim: Oil reserve constraints and data-centre power demand affect living costs.
assessment: Use energy department fuel stocks and AEMO demand/capacity; separate US reserves from Australian import cover.

claim: AI productivity gains spread to wages and jobs.
assessment: Track adoption, output per hour, labour share and real median earnings; higher profits do not automatically become higher wages.
